sections.h: What a ramp rule looks like
sections.flag: Illustrative: my own sketch, not a sourced fact.
p: One hero, one rule. Say the brand color is a mid-lightness green. The rule is a short list: step lightness by a fixed amount per stop, ease chroma down as colors get very light or very dark, and never move hue. Every tint, shade, hover and disabled state is then a calculation, not a decision someone has to remember to make.
Why a rule beats a palette. A hand-built ramp records the answers but not the reasoning. When the brand shifts, the whole ramp has to be redone by eye. A rule keeps the reasoning, so it can be rerun.

sections.h: Where I would not trust it yet
sections.flag: My opinion, based on the tradeoffs above.
p: Wide-gamut hues. A vivid brand color can fall outside what a display can show, and clamping can quietly dull it. For a brand-critical hero shade I would still check it by eye on a few real screens.
Old browsers. If a meaningful share of users cannot read OKLCH, the fallback is a second source of truth to keep in sync. That cost is real, and it is the first thing I would measure.
